The test image is a **microscopic view** (~50 μm scale) showing:
- A central dark brown mass (stroma/conidiophore base)
- Multiple branching, finger-like conidiophores radiating outward
- Oval/elliptical conidia with internal cellular structure visible at tips
- Septate hyphae

Key candidates: **Gray Mold** (Botrytis), **Leaf Mold**, **Early Blight** (Alternaria), **Alternaria_Black_Molds_Stem_Cankers**. Now I'll view one reference per class.
Gray Mold reference is a macro fruit image. Let me now view references from the other top candidates.

All 4 reference views consumed. Now let me synthesize.

**Test image analysis:**
- Microscopic view, 50 μm scale bar
- Central brown mass at base
- Multiple long, septate, branching conidiophores radiating outward in a "bouquet/hand" pattern
- Oval conidia visible at tips (detached examples upper-left and upper-right)
- Conidiophores appear pale/hyaline with cross-walls visible

**Reasoning:**
- The "bouquet" of branched conidiophores bearing oval conidia at tips is the textbook morphology of **Botrytis cinerea** (Gray Mold). The genus name "Botrytis" literally means "bunch of grapes" — the conidia cluster at the tips of repeatedly branched conidiophores.
- The oval conidia size (~10-15 μm at this scale) is consistent with Botrytis (6-18 × 4-11 μm).
- The central brown mass is consistent with the conidiophore base/stipe or a piece of host tissue from which Botrytis conidiophores emerge.
- Alternaria (Early Blight) conidia would be much larger (50-300 μm) with a distinct beak. Leaf Mold (Fulvia fulva) would show conidia in chains with a more fasciculate stomatal emergence pattern. Septoria has filiform pycnidiospores. None fit as well as Botrytis.
- Gray Mold reference images confirm typical macroscopic presentation (fuzzy gray sporulation on stems/fruit), consistent with Botrytis cinerea causing this disease.
